title: The Rebuke of the Wise vs. the Laughter of Fools
english: A person is driven by grief or toward a house of drinking and laughter. The comparison made is such that they choose some things and flee others in many ways, one of which is from those who choose. The wise man chooses virtue, piety, 'to please God', and strives for piety, even if he must die. But the many-sided man, the fool, does not choose these.

From the things chosen, virtue is preferred, because the wise choose it, not the coarse, not the exhausted, not the fool. And from the facts, again the comparison is taken, the beautiful thing said by those judging and comparing. The necessary thing is taken when we say that the soul is more excellent than the body, and it is more fitting to care for it rather than the body. From the matter, toward which the choice and comparison happen, the precious thing is taken, since the soul is more precious. He who is sparing and caring of it cares for the precious and the better according to truth.

And there is also when the preference happens from the things accompanying. Thus it is not necessary to prefer living simply over dying. For even if someone prefers living over the one about to die through clamor or the justice of a judge or something else pursuing Christianity and the truth, it is for a little while. For if he does not die by the murderer, sometimes a disease having seized him interrupts life; it has difference only in time, that he who is immediately subject to the wrath of a judge dies, but to be destroyed by disease, life's end is uncertain, when. However, this is not for an infinity, but in more time he may remain. And thus the judgment happens from the singularity or the speed of the matter.

It is good to hear the rebuke of a wise man rather than the songs of fools. It seems to many that the rebuke from the wise should be avoided, especially when they are lovers of sin. For he having the desire to enjoy and to sin avoids the one forbidding these things. He who has no opinion at all rejoices in flatteries; he wants rather to hear the songs of flattery than the words of rebuke. For it is the part of a wise man to love the one rebuking. For it is said in Proverbs: but the impious and the evil man hates the one rebuking. For he says: 'He who rebukes the impious will be blamed and himself.' For he blames himself, the one [rebuking] the impious...

For the impious man is to be rejected and forbidden. And just as a physician who subjects those unable to be cured by cutting or cautery to such things is not a physician, but an ignorant physician, so he who reproves the incorrigible reproaches himself more, for he provokes them to speak against him.

And they show that one having such a fault does not know whom to reprove and whom not to. Such is the rebuke of the wise over the laughter of fools. Flatterers sing in a certain way; even if they speak moral words, they wish more to please than to benefit those who hear. Laughter is a word that stirs up pleasure, but rebuke, being corrective and persuading one to cease former works, demonstrates them, making it clear that they are things to be avoided and forbidden.

Is it the wise man who rebukes or the one being rebuked? It is the rebuke of the wise, not that which he himself undergoes, but that which he imposes on others. If you wish to take it as 'the rebuke of the wise' being that which he himself undergoes, that is a violent interpretation, yet he says this: the wise man receiving rebuke corrects himself and casts away those things for which the rebuke happened to him, and this is good for him. But he does not mean this, but rather that which he brings to those worthy of rebuke, so that the saying might be similar to this: 'He who brings wisdom from his lips strikes a heartless man with a rod.'

Just as the sound of thorns under a cauldron is so, such is the laughter of fools. And this too is vanity. For the thorns, when they are burned under a cauldron, produce a great noise. And so the laughter of fools is such, until they produce noises; it is not for the sake of refreshing the soul. If the soul does not laugh, it has not yet reached the point of rebuking. Often in the writings, the cauldron signifies punishment. 'For a east wind shall burn from the face of the countenance upon those inhabiting the land' (Ezekiel 20:45), when the people mocked the prophet, they laughed. Fools do not laugh until they have made a noise and sounds; they are more like jesters. And just as the thorns themselves, being burned under the cauldron, emit a noise, so their laughter is from a scorched, evil soul.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Beginning and End of Wisdom
english: Bringing forward those [things]. Furthermore, the upward leading: 'It is good to hear a rebuke from the wise.' The divine word of the Scriptures is wise, and each one of those guarding it is wise according to God, is God-wise. When therefore one such rebukes, is the effort good or not? And he rebukes well. But many rebuke even regarding not allowing someone to be a buffoon, for the sake of not dancing and doing such things. But the wise man brings forward a check against sin. And the rebuke, being such a thing of the wise, being improving, even if the one being improved is not improved, it is good beyond the folly of the foolish, the punishment of the word and not rebuking. And even if a man is harmed through the folly of the foolish, it is not only a woman or a child.

The worldly cares are indeed thorns, the shameful desires, the unrestrained pleasures. This he says: that such things, which those playing the buffoon think they do with pleasure, are thorns, bringing and coming under punishment. And this is vanity. For they will gain nothing from laughter; as you would say to one living badly: 'It is in vain for you.' For slander carries away the wise and destroys the good disposition of his heart. The 'carries away' is thus: often someone accuses the wise man badly and finds many following him. And if he was not entirely well-disposed and perfect, at times he also is shaken.

Susanna, her wise soul not being carried away, was slandered regarding adultery. And the slander was not being said against one or two false accusers; those ruling the people and judges of such accusations were the accusers. All the people paid attention to them as judges and as those ruling the people. And almost no one was a forger of the slander. When therefore, being God-wise, she perceived that in vain the things of the accusation were for her—for she would not find the one listening—she fled to God and with the spoken word she was silent, but with the mind she cried out: 'O God, the Eternal One, the Knower of hidden things, who knows all things before their being, you know that they testify falsely against me.' Slander did not carry her away, nor did it establish her in misery, but it confirmed her in sobriety. And Joseph likewise. And in the time especially of the persecutions, many...

They were flattered and not driven about. Therefore, the wise one here does not speak of the perfect one, but of the one having the beginning, the new one. Thus we have also understood: 'rebuke the wise, and he will love you'. The perfect wise man is not subject to any rebukes. For when it says, 'the wise will not depart from the mouth of the Most High' (Psalm 115:13), it speaks of the perfect ones here.

Many indeed sacrificed without even having a choice, 'the loss of the straightness of their heart'. For it is possible for toil to drive out a heavy intention not entirely all-powerful. A good end of words concerning his beginning, a good long-suffering concerning a high spirit. The end of the words rather has already something good concerning the beginning of the words.

The one beginning the word, in order that you may take the word here as active, the real one, implicitly has it, if he completes the word, if he acts according to the word. title: Knowledge and the Inner Heart
english: He teaches, and he rebukes in a similar way. He does not forbid by one rebuke or a second, but he also approaches health in another way. This long-suffering one is therefore better than the proud and the 'high in spirit'. Indeed, some say that if he speaks more slowly, it is a lesson, saying: 'Ah, a cleansing, go away, you are able to do nothing.' But what of the lifting up? The lifting up is that itself.

Because you desire this: the one believing in the Savior from among the Gentiles is long-suffering, but the people from the circumcision who say, 'We have no king but Caesar' [sic] and 'We are disciples of Moses' are high in spirit. Regarding this one who is high in spirit from the Hebrew people, the one from the Gentiles who became long-suffering because he has known the things concerning him—that 'having no hope and being without God in the world' (1 Thess 4:17; Eph 2:12)—is a precursor there. Do not hasten in a spirit of anger, for anger rests in the foolishness of a mind in a rage.

demonstrating. This one, then, does all things in the soul; but the one having ascended above this and doing with divine reasoning or sometimes with mere reasoning, this one does all things in the spirit.

This, then, I call knowledge, not being knowledge in the strict sense, but that which appears to those using it to be becoming bad. For a fool's passion rests in the heart. The one who is not a fool, but wise and attentive to prudence, even if something is ever seen or heard or moves the passion, it remains only until a passion occurs.

For the heart signifies the ruling principle in many of the divine lessons, as if it says: 'Their folly is in the land of Egypt in their heart' (Ps 106:27). So also it is said in other places that 'all things come into the heart of the unjust' (Prov 14:13). What he says is this: that he touches evils, and against his own ruling principle he brings harm and plague.

Again, if the holy man says: 'My prayer shall turn back into my heart,' the diligent man asks for that, sending a prayer to God, which is both beneficial for him to receive and proper for God to give. And his prayer turns back into his heart, bringing what he asked for. For he asks for nothing more than bodily strength or wealth, but for that which improves the mind.

If, therefore, it happens that what he asks for—since the things given do not remain outside of him, but in his disposition and in the ruling principle—his prayer turns back into his heart. Do not say: 'What happened that the former days were better than these?' (Phil 3:13). 'Better than these' is not merely said, but also reasoned: he who is beginning virtue and 'the illumination of the knowledge of truth' and being shone upon by the 'sun of righteousness' (Mal 4:2) always receives by the light; and just as the diligent man 'stretches toward the prize of the higher calling' (Phil 3:14).

The things being given are left behind, forgetting those from whom they have come, so that he no longer turns back and returns; 'stretching forward to those that are before' (Phil 3:14), he is made distant, he who began to be enlightened by the 'sun of righteousness' (Mal 4:2) and always receives by the light, as if to say that 'the first days were better than these' (Phil 3:13). And we say this somewhat poorly, but perhaps...
